title: Modelling commissioned by the property industry forecasts rents about $9 a week higher and roughly 8,700 fewer homes by 2030 under the changes
oneLiner: The competing estimate, from the groups opposing the bill.
body: Qaive and Tulipwood Economics, commissioned by Master Builders Australia, the Property Council and the Real Estate Institute, forecast rents about $9 a week higher once the changes take effect, several times Treasury's figure, and about 8,700 fewer dwellings by 2029–30. The same modelling credits the budget's supply measures with far fewer homes than Treasury does.
contextBackground: Commissioned by the bill's opponents and rated moderate for that reason. It is the number behind the industry's Senate evidence.
contextDisagreement: Supporters of the bill say the model assumes sold rentals vanish rather than becoming owner-occupied homes; the industry says Treasury assumes frictionless substitution.

evidenceItems.citation: The Nightly, 29 May 2026 — Qaive/Tulipwood modelling for MBA, Property Council and REIA

otherClaim.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market

claimItself.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market
claimItself.oneLiner: Fewer landlords means fewer rentals, and fewer rentals means higher rents.
claimItself.body: If the after-tax return on rental property falls, some investors will sell and fewer will buy. Opponents of reform argue that the resulting withdrawal of rental stock would raise rents for the tenants the policy is meant to help.
